preamble: In French, Vulgar Latin /ɛ/ in a closed syllable before a nasal consonant was nasalized (Early Old French [ɛ̃]) and then lowered, probably in the 11th or early 12th century, merging with nasal /ã/; the nasal consonant was later lost. The net result is ɛ → ã (Parisian [ɑ̃], Canadian [ã]), reached through an intermediate [ɛ̃] stage. The lowering did not affect Old Norman or Anglo-Norman, and it was blocked in the sequences /jẽ/ and /ẽj/ (bien, plein). No independent case outside French has been found.

examples.note: Closed-syllable /ɛn/ gave /ã/, later /ɑ̃/ in Parisian French after loss of the nasal consonant.

examples.from: Latin ventus 'wind' (Vulgar Latin /ɛ/, cf. Italian vento /ˈvɛnto/)
examples.note: Same development in the same environment.

examples.to: Old French tens, tans > French temps /tɑ̃/ (France), /tã/ (Quebec)
examples.note: The Old French spelling tans already shows the lowered vowel.
